Clinical Observations
A Rare Case of Childhood Stiff Person Syndrome Associated With
Pleuropulmonary Blastoma
Hyun-Ok Jun MD a, Mi-Sun Yum MD a, Eun-Hee Kim MD a, Yun-Jeong Lee MD a,
Jong-Jin Seo MD b, Tae-Sung Ko MD a, *
a Division of Pediatric Neurology, Department of Pediatrics, Asan Medical Center Children ’s Hospital, University of Ulsan College of
Medicine, Seoul, Korea
b Division of Pediatric Hemato-oncology, Department of Pediatrics, Asan Medical Center Children ’s Hospital, University of Ulsan
College of Medicine, Seoul, Korea
abstract
INTRODUCTION: Stiff person syndrome is a rare autoimmune, neurological disorder characterized by progressive
rigidity and episodic painful spasms, predominantly affecting the proximal limbs and axial muscles, and leading to
progressive disability. We report the case of a child who developed symptoms compatible with stiff person
syndrome during treatment for pleuropulmonary blastoma.
PATIENT DESCRIPTION: A 3-year, 5-month-old girl was
admitted for gradually worsening postural tremor, painful spasms, and generalized stiffness. Since the age of 3
years, she had been on adjuvant chemotherapy for pleuropulmonary blastoma before surgical resection. Brain
magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalographic ﬁndings were normal. Although serologic tests for
autoimmune disease, including paraneoplastic antibodies and antiglutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies, were
unremarkable, her ﬁndings were attributed to a paraneoplastic syndrome based on her clinical features and
medical history. However, following the planned pulmonary lobectomy, her symptoms were paradoxically
aggravated, with continuous motor unit potential at rest on electromyography, which occurs in stiff person syn-
drome. She gradually improved during postadjuvant chemotherapy with simultaneous immunotherapy including
intravenous immunoglobulins and methylprednisolone, and she had recovered completely when evaluated at the
22-month follow-up visit after completion of her treatment for pleuropulmonary blastoma.
CONCLUSION: We
present the ﬁrst documented child with stiff person syndrome associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma. The
marked clinical improvement following chemotherapy for pleuropulmonary blastoma was yet more proof of the
pleuropulmonary blastoma-related stiff person syndrome. In children with a malignancy and stiff person syn-
drome, a paraneoplastic syndrome should be considered and the treatment for the malignancy must be
undertaken.
Keywords: stiff person syndrome, stiff man syndrome, pleuropulmonary blastoma, paraneoplastic syndrome

Introduction
Stiff person syndrome is a rare, insidiously progressive
autoimmune neurological disorder characterized by
stiffness in the axial and proximal limb muscles and
superimposed stimulus-sensitive axial and appendicular
spasms.1 It was ﬁrst described in 1956 by Moersch and
Woltman.2
Although the exact etiology of stiff person syndrome is
still unclear, autoantibodies against glutamic acid decar-
boxylase (GAD), the enzyme responsible for the synthesis of
g-aminobutyric acid (GABA), are reported in approximately
60% to 80% of stiff person syndrome patients, and thus
suggesting the signi ﬁcant role of the immune system in the
pathogenesis of stiff person syndrome.
3,4 The functional

impairment may result from the immunological destruction
of inhibitory interneurons, reduction of the presynaptic
neurotransmitter synthesis, or decreased number of the
postsynaptic receptors.
1 Only 5% of stiff person syndrome
patients have speci ﬁc malignancies, 1 and most of these
patients are positive for autoantibodies directed against
amphiphysin.
5,6 Breast cancer, thymoma, Hodgkin lym-
phoma, small-cell lung carcinoma, and colon cancer 7 have
been reported in adults with paraneoplastic stiff person
syndrome.
5,6
We describe a child who developed symptoms compat-
ible to those of stiff person syndrome during treatment for
pleuropulmonary blastoma. Stiff person syndrome associ-
ated with malignancy in the literature. Moreover, this is the
ﬁrst patient with a documented paraneoplastic neurological
syndrome associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma.
Patient Description
This 3-year, 5-month-old girl was admitted for gradually worsening
postural tremor, painful spasms of both the hands and lower extremities,
and generalized stiffness that had developed 2 months previously. At age
3 years, she had been diagnosed with pleuropulmonary blastoma in her
left hemithorax and then began adjuvant chemotherapy
for pleuropulmonary blastoma for one month before undergoing surgi-
cal resection. A huge lung mass was seen on a chest computed tomog-
raphy scan that was performed to evaluate prolonged fever just before
the diagnosis of pleuropulmonary blastoma ( Fig 1 A). Her birth and
developmental history and her family ’s medical history were
unremarkable.
Her symptoms began as tightness in the upper limbs and deterio-
rated into muscle stiffness of the trunk that was reduced during sleep.
She also suffered from bilateral arm tremors and uncontrolled falls
without loss of consciousness. There was no diurnal ﬂuctuation in these
falling attacks. Physical examination showed truncal stiffness and ri-
gidity of both the arms and the legs that was more severe in the right arm
than in the left. Because of severe leg stiffness, she was completely un-
able to walk. However, cranial nerve examination, the cerebellar function
test, and deep tendon re ﬂexes at all sites were normal.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography,
performed to evaluate for seizures, were unremarkable. Serologic tests
for autoimmune disease, including anti-GAD antibodies and paraneo-
plastic or other autoimmune disease-related antibodies, such as anti-Hu,
anti-Yo, anti-Ri, anti-Tg, anti-thyroid peroxidase, thyroid-stimulating
hormone receptor, and neuromyelitis optica antibody, were unremark-
able. Serologic test for antiamphiphysin antibody or antiglycin receptor
antibody was not done. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid did not contain autoimmune
antibodies, including anti-GAD antibodies. Despite the absence of sero-
logic abnormalities, her tremor and spasticity were attributed to a par-
aneoplastic syndrome based on her clinical features and medical history.
Therefore, pleuropulmonary blastoma treatment was continued with
medication including dantrolene, baclofen, and diazepam to control her
symptoms.
According to the therapeutic plan for pleuropulmonary blastoma,
she underwent pulmonary lobectomy two months following the onset of
her neurological symptoms. However, after her lobectomy, her symp-
toms were paradoxically aggravated and she experienced generalized
stiffness with swallowing dif ﬁculties and dysarthria. At that time, she

could not sit or change her position by herself and could only control her
facial muscles and ﬁngertips. The electromyography showed prominent,
continuous motor unit potential at rest in the right gastrocnemius, right
tibialis anterior, left trapezius, and left biceps brachii, ﬁndings typical of
stiff person syndrome ( Fig 2 ). With her diagnosis of paraneoplastic stiff
person syndrome, we continued her chemotherapy for pleuropulmonary
blastoma with simultaneous immunotherapy including intravenous
immunoglobulins (400 mg/kg for 5 days) and methylprednisolone
(30 mg/kg for 4 days). She gradually improved during the postadjuvant
chemotherapy. Her symptoms gradually resolved, her spasms and falling
attacks disappeared, and she could ﬁnally sit and move her upper limbs
by herself.
At age 4 years and 3 months, after completing chemotherapy, she
tapered her antispasmodic medications and no rigidity or spasms
remained. At her 22-month follow-up examination after completion of
her pleuropulmonary blastoma treatment, she had recovered completely
without any motor or cognitive de ﬁcits.
Discussion
Stiff person syndrome is a rare disorder among adults,
typically ﬁrst presenting in the fourth to sixth decades of
life.1 The characteristic of classical stiff person syndrome in
adulthood is chronic, slow progression of the clinical course
over months or years, and anti-GAD antibodies were found
in most patients.
8 In comparison, published reports of pe-
diatric stiff person syndrome have been rare, 9 and the pa-
tients described in the previous articles had some
characteristic features. First, they had severe phenotypes,
more frequently involving the whole body. Second, positive
serological reports of autoimmune antibody in childhood
stiff person syndrome are rarely found when compared with
those of adults.
9 In addition, childhood stiff person syn-
drome exhibits an acute onset and a relatively benign course
with clinical improvement and less disability following
therapy.8-10
Stiff person syndrome is considered to be an autoim-
mune disease because the majority of stiff person syndrome
patients already have the diagnosis of an autoimmune
disease. Approximately 70% of stiff person syndrome pa-
tients have serum autoantibodies against GAD and many of
them experience systemic autoimmune disorders such as
insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.
11
Although the role of autoimmunity against GAD in the
pathogenesis of stiff person syndrome is still unclear, the
central key to the pathophysiology of stiff person syndrome
is thought to be impaired GABAergic and glycinergic
synaptic transmission resulting from autoantibodies.
1
In particular, in patients with accompanying malignancy,
antiamphiphysin antibodies are frequently detected and
thought to have a role in their autoimmunity. Although
we could not assess the antiamphiphysin antibodies in our

patient, no other autoantibodies, including anti-GAD or
paraneoplastic antibodies, were detected. There are two
possible explanations. First, the presence of pathogenic
mechanisms other than autoimmunity (e.g., T-cell mediated
neuronal injury) can be assumed. In the previous study of a
breast cancer eassociated stiff person syndrome patient,
histopathology of the brainstem, spinal cord, and mesial
temporal lobe structure revealed perivascular and paren-
chymal lymphocytic in ﬁltrates mediated by CD8
þ T cells
and microglia.12
Second, stiff person syndrome could be caused by un-
known autoantibodies. In paraneoplastic neurological

continuous motor unit potential at rest during chemotherapy for pleuropulmonary blastoma. Lt, left; Rt, right.

syndromes, onconeural coimmunity is considered the
principal pathological mechanism. 13 Pleuropulmonary
blastoma is a very rare cancer in children and has never
been reported in association with paraneoplastic stiff
person syndrome. Therefore, a novel, unknown onco-
neural antibody can be associated with stiff person syn-
drome in this patient.
In 65% to 70% of patients with paraneoplastic neurological
syndrome, the neurological symptoms appears before the
diagnosis of malignancy.
14,15 However, a neurological syn-
drome in patients with cancer diagnosed withintwo years
can be diagnosed as possible paraneoplastic neurological
syndrome.
15 In our patient, the neurological symptoms
developed after the initiation of chemotherapy, suggesting
that of immunological alteration by the chemotherapy or the
chemotherapy itself could constitute a provocative factor of
stiff person syndrome. Iwata et al. reported an acute relapse
of stiff person syndrome after a traumatic stimulation event
such as surgical intervention.
16 Transiently increased pro-
duction of paraneoplastic mediators after chemotherapy or
surgical intervention could explain the clinical exacerbation
in this child.
In the current treatment for stiff person syndrome,
immunomodulation including plasmapheresis, intravenous
immunoglobulins or corticosteroids is used to remove or
counter the pathogenic antibodies, and symptomatic anti-
spasmodic management is included to enhance GABAergic
neurotransmission.
17 In general, drugs that promote
GABAergic inhibition, such as benzodiazepines (diazepam
and clonazepam) and baclofen, can diminish the severity of
the spasms and stiffness.
17
However, for paraneoplastic stiff person syndrome,
several authors have recommended that treatment for ma-
lignancy should be accompanied by immunotherapy and
symptomatic therapy.18 The variable response rate of pedi-
atric stiff person syndrome patients to immunotherapy may
reﬂect progression of the disease during the delay in
implementing immunotherapy or different pathophysio-
logical mechanisms in individual patients.
9
Because of its rarity, stiff person syndrome is frequently
misdiagnosed. Clardy et al. estimated that the average dis-
ease duration before the diagnosis of stiff person syndrome
was 14 years, and two patients were diagnosed as having a
psychological disorder causing their symptoms.
9 The rarity
of pediatric stiff person syndrome as well as the overlapping
clinical features of this disorder with those of other
neurological diseases may prevent its early recognition.
Nonetheless, recognition of stiff person syndrome is
important because this is a treatable disorder.
Conclusion
This is the ﬁrst reported child with paraneoplastic stiff
person syndrome associated with pleuropulmonary blas-
toma. In children with stiff person syndrome or progressive
rigidity and myoclonus, the diagnosis of paraneoplastic
syndrome and malignancy screening should be considered.
Moreover, clinicians should be aware that acute exacerba-
tion of symptoms can occur during the chemotherapy or
after surgical intervention. In the treatment of stiff person
syndrome, treatment for the malignancy should be accom-
panied by immunotherapy.
